title: Minimum spanning tree: edge-subset enumeration vs Kruskal (and Prim)
problem_statement: Given the complete undirected graph K_n on n >= 1 vertices with positive integer edge weights (a symmetric n x n weight matrix), compute the total weight of a minimum spanning tree. For n = 1 the answer is 0.

input.size_measure: m = n(n-1)/2 edge weights (Theta(n^2) input), integers below 10^9 in the harness, so arithmetic and comparisons are unit cost.

algorithms.name: enumeration of all (n-1)-edge subsets
algorithms.idea: Every spanning tree has exactly n-1 edges. Try each of the C(n(n-1)/2, n-1) subsets of n-1 edges; it is a spanning tree iff it connects all n vertices (one depth-first search). Keep the lightest.
algorithms.pseudocode: for each (n-1)-subset T of the edges: if T is connected: best = min(best, weight(T))
algorithms.time_complexity: Theta(n * C(n(n-1)/2, n-1)) = 2^Theta(n log n) (C(m, n-1) subsets, Theta(n) each to build, search and weigh)
algorithms.correctness: Exhaustive. A graph with n vertices and n-1 edges is a tree iff it is connected, so the connected subsets are exactly the spanning trees.

algorithms.name: Kruskal with union-find
algorithms.idea: Sort the edges by weight and scan them, keeping each edge that joins two different components (tracked by union-find with union by size and path halving).
algorithms.time_complexity: O(m log m) = O(n^2 log n) on K_n (comparison sort of the m edges; the union-find work is O(m alpha(n)))
algorithms.correctness: Kruskal 1956. Cut property: the lightest edge crossing a cut that respects the current forest belongs to some minimum spanning tree containing that forest, so every edge kept is safe. Edges inside a component would close a cycle and are skipped.

shape.note: comparisons inside sorted() (RL-069); also count depends on the drawn instance; kept so the record says why the diagnostic cannot decide

algorithms.name: Prim, array version
algorithms.idea: Grow one tree from vertex 0. Keep for every outside vertex the cheapest edge to the tree; each round adds the closest outside vertex and updates the others by scanning its row.
algorithms.time_complexity: Theta(n^2) on K_n (n-1 rounds, two Theta(n) scans each), linear in the input size
algorithms.correctness: Prim 1957. Each round adds the lightest edge crossing the cut (tree, rest), which is safe by the cut property.

relationship: Super-exponential -> polynomial: Theta(n * C(n(n-1)/2, n-1)) = 2^Theta(n log n) vs O(n^2 log n) (Kruskal) and Theta(n^2) (Prim, linear in the input on dense graphs). The cut property makes greedy choices safe, so no search is needed. Even enumerating only the spanning trees would not help: K_n has n^(n-2) of them (Cayley's formula). On sparse graphs the line continues with Chazelle 2000 (O(m alpha(m, n)), deterministic) and Karger-Klein-Tarjan 1995 (expected O(m), randomized).

A minimum spanning tree algorithm with inverse-Ackermann type complexity

verification.method: V1: all three implementations agree for n = 1..7 (enumeration capped at n = 7, i.e. 54,264 subsets) on random weights in [1, 100] and, in some trials, in [1, 3] (many ties); Kruskal and Prim also agree at n = 20, 60 and 200. harness.check is independent of all three: Boruvka's algorithm with (w, u, v) tie-breaking, plus the bounds (sum of the n-1 lightest edges) <= answer <= (weight of the path 0-1-...-(n-1)). V2 by exact operation counts (measure 'reported', round 2026-10-06c) on weights in [1, 10^9], with the same seeded draws as the earlier timing fit. generate_scaling wraps every off-diagonal weight in an instrumented type that counts each comparison and each arithmetic operation (+, *, divmod) with an input weight as an operand. Kruskal's packed key w*n^2 + u*n + v is then itself an instrumented value, so the comparisons made inside sorted() call its __lt__ and are counted. The implementations are unchanged and return the same MST weights on the counting type (experiments/2026-10-06c_mst_counts.py). Kruskal: count = 3m packing operations + sort comparisons + one divmod per scanned key (m = n(n-1)/2), cross-checked against sorted() applied to the same keys and a replay of the scan on plain ints; 14811, 69526, 319007, 1438399, 6400007 for n = 50..800 under Python 3.14.2 (1.095-1.179 m log2 m; see caveats for 3.12); alpha = 0.998 against n^2 log n at tolerance 0.03, rivals n^2 (1.094), n^2 log^2 n (0.917) and n^3 (0.729) rejected, so the log factor is resolved. Prim: exactly (n-1)(n-2) comparisons + (n-1) additions = (n-1)^2; alpha = 1.007 against n^2, rivals n^2 log n (0.918) and n^3 (0.671) rejected. Enumeration: exactly (n-1) C(m, n-1) additions + n^(n-2) - 1 comparisons (one per spanning tree after the first; Cayley's formula), 75, 964, 16310, 342390 for n = 4..7; alpha = 0.995 against n C(m, n-1), rivals C(m, n-1) (1.065), n^2 C(m, n-1) (0.934) and n^(n-2) (1.210) rejected. Not counted: the union-find operations (on plain vertex ints) and the enumeration's depth-first search. Timing history: an earlier Kruskal version that sorted (w, u, v) tuples measured alpha ~1.19, attributed to cache effects once m exceeds ~10^5 edges (the cause was not tested); packing each edge into one integer key (same sort order) removed this. The timing fit could not resolve Kruskal's log factor.

caveats: On K_n Prim's Theta(n^2) array version is already optimal up to a constant factor among deterministic algorithms: an adversary that answers 2 to every weight query can still give any unread edge weight 1, which lowers the answer from 2(n - 1) to 2n - 3 (n >= 2; the edge lies on a spanning tree whose other n - 2 edges weigh 2), so every correct algorithm reads all n(n-1)/2 weights. For Kruskal only the upper bound O(n^2 log n) is stated (no worst-case lower bound is proved here); on the V2 draws its counts grow like n^2 log n, and the V2 counts resolve the log factor on these draws: n^2 is rejected for Kruskal and n^2 log n for Prim. Kruskal's count includes the comparisons made inside CPython's sorted() (Timsort), so its exact values depend on the sort implementation of the Python version; under CPython 3.12.10 the Kruskal counts are 0.17-0.30% lower than under 3.14.2 (14766 vs 14811 at n = 50, 6388918 vs 6400007 at n = 800), only in the sort comparisons, with alpha = 0.998 under both versions and the same verdicts. The other count series of this entry are identical under both versions. The counts leave out the union-find work and the enumeration's depth-first search.
notes: The enumeration's count C(n(n-1)/2, n-1) grows like (e n / 2)^(n-1) up to polynomial factors; only n^(n-2) of these subsets are spanning trees (Cayley's formula). Secondary tag T3 (RL-056): Kruskal Theta(m log m) = Theta(n^2 log n) on K_n -> Prim Theta(n^2). The log factor rests on the comparison-sorting lower bound, which is background and not proved here; on the V2 draws the exact counts resolve it as a measurement.
